pre_post_comparison.Timed Up and Go: baseline 31 s; 2 hours 24 s (23% faster); 24 hours 21 s (32% faster)

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Evans index 0.35, increased from 0.30; callosal angle 82 degrees; temporal horn enlargement; incomplete DESH; patent aqueduct, no obstruction; 1.2 cm right frontal encephalomalacia, microhaemorrhages and superficial siderosis
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI for progressive communicating ventriculomegaly and the traumatic changes
action_criteria.rationale: Compared with the 3-month study, the MRI shows whether the ventricles are enlarging in a communicating pattern rather than settling ex vacuo, and excludes obstruction before CSF is removed.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal blood count, coagulation, sodium, creatinine, TSH and B12; glucose 108 mg/dL
action_criteria.label: Targeted labs for reversible contributors
action_criteria.rationale: Nothing in this post-traumatic course points to a metabolic mimic, so labs only document routine safety before the tap.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 31 s with walker, 10-m walk 24 s in 27 steps, 180-degree turn in 8 steps, freezing at transitions and retropulsion
action_criteria.label: Baseline timed gait assessment before the tap
action_criteria.rationale: The decline from walker-assisted walking needs timed baseline values before CSF removal, or the tap response cannot be measured.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MoCA 19/30 with slowing, executive and attentional deficits and cued recall benefit
action_criteria.label: Bedside cognitive screen (MoCA)
action_criteria.rationale: A baseline MoCA quantifies the slowing that the family describes as worsening and gives a second measure for the tap.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Opening pressure 14 cmH2O with normal cells, protein and glucose; after 40 mL, TUG 31 to 24 s at 2 hours and 21 s at 24 hours (32%), 10-m walk 24 to 17 s, MoCA 19 to 22
action_criteria.label: CSF tap test with opening pressure
action_criteria.rationale: The tap separates a shunt-responsive post-traumatic hydrocephalus from static diffuse axonal injury, which the trajectory alone cannot do.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 24 s at 2 hours and 21 s at 24 hours (32% faster), 10-m walk 17 s in 21 steps, MoCA 22/30
action_criteria.label: Post-tap timed gait reassessment
action_criteria.rationale: Repeating the same timed measures at 2 and 24 hours turns the CSF removal into a test of shunt responsiveness.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform large-volume lumbar puncture before MRI excludes mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute a progressive decline months after the injury to static TBI sequelae or depression without excluding communicating hydrocephalus
Do not attribute the ventricular enlargement to ex-vacuo change from the small right frontal contusion: the ventricles are enlarging out of proportion to the focal lesion and the cortical volume loss
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve for post-traumatic communicating hydrocephalus after the severe TBI with traumatic subarachnoid and intraventricular haemorrhage, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 32% in TUG at 24 hours, the enlarging ventricles (Evans index 0.30 to 0.35, callosal angle 82 degrees) and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]
Continue sertraline and address post-TBI depression in parallel, as a contributor to slowing that shunting will not treat
Counsel the patient and family that shunting is expected to reverse the recent decline but not the cognitive deficit from the diffuse axonal injury documented at 3 months
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizures or fluctuating awareness are reported after the injury, so an EEG cannot inform the decline.
His two falls came with the gait decline, without syncope or palpitations, so an ECG does not inform the work-up.
No syncope, murmur or embolic event is reported, so echocardiography has no role in a post-traumatic gait decline.
The falls are gait falls without syncope or palpitations; rhythm monitoring has no role.
A head CT was done 2 weeks ago and MRI is available; another CT adds nothing to the ventricular and traumatic assessment.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the decision, which rests on serial MRI and the tap test.
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are.
Normal CSF cells and an afebrile post-traumatic course give no reason for prion, inflammatory or infectious CSF assays.

differential.diagnosis: Static sequelae of diffuse axonal injury
differential.key_features: Diffuse axonal injury explains the deficit documented at 3 months, but static sequelae do not worsen 5 to 8 months after the injury, and the gait improved 32% after CSF removal.

differential.diagnosis: Post-traumatic ventriculomegaly ex vacuo (atrophy after diffuse axonal injury)
differential.key_features: Cortical volume loss is only mild while the Evans index rose from 0.30 to 0.35 with an acute callosal angle, enlarged temporal horns and a tap response.

differential.diagnosis: Post-TBI depression with pseudodementia and psychomotor slowing
differential.key_features: Depression is treated and contributes to slowing, but it does not cause a magnetic gait, incontinence or enlarging ventricles, and the MoCA rose 3 points after CSF removal.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic small-vessel disease
differential.key_features: White matter change is Fazekas 1 without lacunes and cannot explain the enlarging ventricles or the tap response.
The imaging and tap response match, but onset within months of a TBI with subarachnoid and intraventricular blood is an antecedent that makes the hydrocephalus secondary.

differential.diagnosis: Focal encephalomalacia-related cognitive and gait deficits
differential.key_features: A 1.2 cm unilateral right frontal focus cannot explain a bilateral magnetic gait, incontinence or progressive ventricular enlargement.

key_clinical_evidence: Post-traumatic communicating hydrocephalus follows severe TBI with subarachnoid or intraventricular blood, usually within months, by impaired CSF absorption; with normal opening pressure it behaves as secondary normal pressure hydrocephalus and is shunted by the same route.
The trajectory is the pivot: static sequelae of diffuse axonal injury plateau or improve, while this patient deteriorated in gait, cognition and continence 3 to 8 months after the injury.

Serial MRI shows the Evans index rising from 0.30 to 0.35 with an acute callosal angle (82 degrees), enlarged temporal horns and a patent aqueduct, against only mild cortical volume loss, which argues against an ex-vacuo process.

Opening pressure 14 cmH2O with normal CSF content; after 40 mL, TUG improved 23% at 2 hours and 32% at 24 hours with concordant 10-m walk and MoCA changes. A 10% or greater TUG improvement is a commonly used positive criterion; tap-test sensitivity is 26% to 61% and PPV 73% to 100% [Marmarou_2005].
Treated post-TBI depression and the small right frontal contusion are real but cannot explain the progressive magnetic gait, incontinence or ventricular enlargement.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Diffuse axonal injury and depression explain a static or improving deficit, not a progressive magnetic gait, new incontinence and enlarging ventricles months after the injury.
red_herrings.data_point: Post-TBI depression on sertraline with 'moderate cognitive impairment consistent with diffuse axonal injury' documented at the 3-month neuropsychology assessment
red_herrings.intended_effect: The agent attributes the progressive slowing and gait decline to static TBI sequelae and depression rather than to a treatable communicating hydrocephalus

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The right frontal encephalomalacic focus is small and unilateral; it cannot account for a bilateral magnetic gait, incontinence or progressive communicating ventriculomegaly.
red_herrings.data_point: Focal encephalomalacia, 1.2 cm, with haemosiderin rim on SWI (right frontal subcortical white matter)
red_herrings.intended_effect: The agent anchors on the focal TBI lesion and concludes the deficits are irreversible

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]
The timed gait is repeated after the tap, at 2 to 24 hours, so that its change from the baseline measures the response to CSF removal [Nakajima_2021]

mri.impression: 1. Communicating ventriculomegaly (Evans index 0.35, increased from 0.30 five months earlier) with an acute callosal angle of 82 degrees, temporal horn enlargement and no obstructing lesion; incomplete DESH pattern (tight high-convexity sulci without Sylvian enlargement). 2. metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Post-traumatic secondary normal pressure hydrocephalus 8 months after severe TBI with traumatic SAH and IVH: static-sequelae and depression anchoring, a small focal contusion distractor, and serial MRI showing enlarging ventricles.
metadata.revision_reason: case-level re-audit of all NPH reviewer requests: the tap report is routed to CSF, timed gait/cognitive assessment is the required pre/post measure, the standalone neuropsychological battery and advanced imaging are removed from gold actions and callable authored follow-ups, laboratories remain optional, unrelated CSF assays are no longer returned for free, and the unsupported universal 20% response threshold is corrected

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive gait deterioration, cognitive slowing, and urinary incontinence worsening over 6 months after severe traumatic brain injury

past_medical_history: Severe traumatic brain injury (motor vehicle collision, 8 months ago): diffuse axonal injury with traumatic subarachnoid and intraventricular haemorrhage; GCS 6 at the scene; 12 days of ICU care, no surgical intervention

social_history.living_situation: Lives with wife and adult son
social_history.tobacco: Former smoker, quit 10 years ago (20 pack-years)

patient.history_present_illness: A 64-year-old right-handed man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes sustained a severe traumatic brain injury 8 months ago in a motor vehicle collision (passenger). He had diffuse axonal injury with traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage and intraventricular haemorrhage. GCS was 6 at the scene; he required 12 days of ICU care but no neurosurgical intervention. After discharge he underwent 3 months of inpatient rehabilitation and was walking with a walker by 3 months after the injury. His neuropsychology report at 3 months noted 'moderate cognitive impairment consistent with diffuse axonal injury'. His physiatrist attributed his ongoing slowing to the brain injury and depression, and his psychiatrist started sertraline 3 months ago. His wife reports that over the past 5 to 6 months, instead of the expected gradual improvement, he has deteriorated: his gait has gone from walker-assisted community walking to needing assistance at all times, he has fallen twice in the past 2 months, his thinking has slowed further rather than plateauing, and he has developed urinary urgency with incontinence requiring pads. His primary care physician obtained a head CT 2 weeks ago, reported as showing enlarged ventricles, and referred him for inpatient evaluation of the decline. The MRI obtained at the rehabilitation hospital 3 months after the injury had documented resolution of the intraventricular haemorrhage, with the Evans index at 0.30.

neurological_exam.additional: No cogwheel rigidity. No resting tremor. Pull test: 3 steps backward, does not fall unassisted. No nuchal rigidity. No orthostatic hypotension on standing.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact bilaterally. Heel-shin mildly awkward bilaterally. No appendicular ataxia.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, short-stepped, shuffling gait with a magnetic quality and reduced foot clearance; en-bloc turning in many small steps; freezing at doorways. No festination. Walks with a walker and standby assistance.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person and place, disoriented to date; markedly slowed processing; formal cognitive screening reported separately. No aphasia; word-finding intact.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal strength throughout bilaterally. Mildly increased tone bilateral lower extremities. No focal weakness. No tremor.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ throughout bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Vibration mildly reduced at ankles bilaterally. Joint position sense intact. No asymmetric deficit.
